title: External Enablement Across Types of Environmental Change: Experimental Evidence on Onset Variance Effects
authors: Jiyoung Kim; Per Davidsson; Denis A. Grégoire
affiliations: University of Queensland, Queensland, Australia; Jönköping International Business School, Jönköping, Sweden; Australian Centre for Entrepreneurship Research, Queensland University of Technology, Queensland, Australia; HEC Montréal, Québec, Canada
abstract: A growing research stream applies the external enablement framework (EEF) to capture how macroenvironmental changes benefit entrepreneurial pursuits. To refine and nuance the EEF’s guidance of future research in this domain, we examine the provisionally suggested structural relationships among its constructs. Combining between-subjects experiments and think-aloud protocols, we show that variance in the characteristics of macroenvironmental changes—specifically, their gradual versus radical onset—influences expectations of enablement and does so similarly across types of change. Our results also uncover relationships between macroenvironmental changes and agents beyond what the EEF explicates. We discuss implications for future research on macroenvironmental impact on business.

authors: Victor Cui; Qian Xiang; Jiatao Li; Jianqi Zhang
affiliations: Conrad School of Entrepreneurship and Business University of Waterloo Waterloo Ontario Canada; School of Finance and Economics Guangdong Polytechnic Normal University Guangzhou China; School of Business and Management Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Clear Water Bay Hong Kong; Lingnan College Sun Yat‐sen University Guangzhou China
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Anecdotes suggest that multinational enterprises (MNEs) from weak intellectual property rights (IPR) regimes often leapfrog to technological leadership by recruiting talent in advanced host countries. Yet whether—and how—such a strategy works remains unclear. Using data on 486 MNEs from 29 countries operating in the United States and interviews with skilled inventors, we uncover a paradox in the springboard‐via‐hiring logic: externally, weak home‐country IPR reputation deters skilled inventors from joining, limiting recruitment; internally, even when talent is hired, home‐country‐imprinted IPR routines constrain post‐hire learning, yielding incremental improvements. These effects are mitigated by firm‐specific exposure to host‐country patent infringement litigation. Our research suggests that springboard‐via‐hiring is institution‐based, contingent on both home‐ and host‐country IPR regimes. These findings offer implications for technology policy and MNEs' strategy amid geopolitical tension. Managerial Summary Can multinational enterprises (MNEs) from weak intellectual property rights (IPR) regimes leapfrog by hiring technical talent in advanced economies? Evidence on 486 MNEs from 29 countries operating in the US high‐technology sector suggests: weaker home‐country IPR reputations make it harder to attract skilled inventors; even after hiring, home‐imprinted IPR routines can constrain recruits' knowledge transfer, often steering outcomes toward incremental improvements. These home‐country constraints are, however, mitigated by firm‐specific exposure to US patent infringement litigation. The springboard‐via‐hiring strategy is thus institution‐based, contingent on both home‐ and host‐country IPR regimes. We accordingly offer advice on technology policy and global R&D strategies for host‐country governments and MNEs amid geopolitical tension.

title: Democratic Organizing and Contemporary Managerial Talent Markets: Internal Promotion or External Hiring?
authors: Aleksandra Gregoric; Takao Kato; Casper B. L. Larsen
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Department of Accounting, Center for Corporate Governance and Owner-Managed Firms, Frederiksberg, Denmark; Colgate University, Department of Economics, Hamilton, New York, United States; Copenhagen Business School, Department of Accounting, Center for Corporate Governance, Frederiksberg, Capital Region, Denmark
abstract: We develop and empirically examine a theoretical framework explaining the relationship between democratic organizing and firms’ propensity to staff management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. Conventionally, the advantages of promoting through internal labor markets (ILM) have rested on the assumption that workers value intra-firm careers and anticipate remaining with the same employer for a longer term. These advantages may prove harder to attain in contemporary labor markets, given that declining tenure and workers’ growing preference for inter-firm careers possibly reduce the information advantage of ILM and undermine internal candidate retention. We propose that firms with more democratic organizing are less susceptible to these ILM challenges, enjoy higher benefits from recruiting internally and are thus more likely to fill management positions through internal promotion. Using longitudinal employer-employee linked data for Danish firms from 2001 to 2017, we find that firms with worker board representation (WBR), one form of more democratic organizing, are more likely than firms without WBR to fill management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. This association is stronger where (i) worker representatives have broader intra-firm experience and are more likely to possess promotion-relevant information; (ii) more managers and professionals have peers serving as worker representatives on the board. These results are consistent with a higher economic viability of internal promotion in firms with more democratic organizing, and largely inconsistent with the conventional account of powerful workers distorting firms’ hiring choices. Interviews with worker directors and human resource professionals illustrate the proposed mechanisms.
abs_publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences

title: Embedded in Two Worlds: How Incumbents’ Brokerage Affects Adaptation When Old and New Supply Networks Coexist
authors: Jongyoun Baek; Andrew V. Shipilov; Nathan R. Furr
affiliations: INSEAD, EFE, Fontainebleau, Île-de-France, France; INSEAD, Strategy, Fontainebleau, France
abstract: The development of new technology architectures often opens up new markets within an existing industry. Incumbents face the decision of whether to enter the new technology market and how to do so. As incumbents attempt to enter the new market, they can become embedded in two buyer-supplier networks, one for the old and the other for new technologies. We argue that brokers have an advantage in this process because they have developed capabilities to integrate suppliers of new technology components or develop unique component combinations for the new technology products. In a study of the U.S. automotive industry between 2012 and 2022, we find that brokerage in the old technology network is positively associated with successful entry into the new technology (i.e., number and performance of new technology models). Surprisingly, brokerage in the old technology network had a stronger positive impact than brokerage in the new technology network on incumbents’ entry into the new technology market for electric vehicles.

title: Throttling Equilibria in Auction Markets
authors: Xi Chen; Christian Kroer; Rachitesh Kumar
affiliations: Columbia University, Computer Science Department, New York, New York, United States; Columbia University, IEOR, New York, New York, United States; Carnegie Mellon University, Tepper School of Business, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: Throttling is a popular method of budget management for online ad auctions in which the platform modulates the participation probability of an advertiser in order to smoothly spend her budget across many auctions. In this work, we investigate the setting in which all of the advertisers simultaneously employ throttling to manage their budgets, and we do so for both first-price and second-price auctions. We analyze the structural and computational properties of the resulting equilibria. For first-price auctions, we show that a unique equilibrium always exists, is well-behaved and can be computed efficiently via tatonnement-style decentralized dynamics. In contrast, for second-price auctions, we prove that even though an equilibrium always exists, the problem of finding even an approximate equilibrium is PPAD-complete, there can be multiple equilibria, and it is NP-hard to find the revenue maximizing one. We also compare the equilibrium outcomes of throttling to those of multiplicative pacing, which is the other most popular and well-studied method of budget management. Finally, we characterize the Price of Anarchy of these equilibria for liquid welfare by showing that it is at most 2 for both first-price and second-price auctions, and demonstrating that our bound is tight.

title: Reducing Risk Through Trade Credit: Theory and Evidence from Dual-Channel Suppliers
authors: Jie Ning; Sammi Y. Tang; Jing Wu; Jiaqi Zhu
affiliations: Department of Operations, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, Ohio 44106; Department of Management, University of Miami, Coral Gables, Florida 33146; CUHK Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Tilburg School of Economics and Management, Tilburg University, Tilburg 5037AB, Netherlands
abstract: Trade credit is traditionally viewed as increasing supplier risk, because delayed payments expose suppliers to buyer uncertainties. Using a stylized game-theoretic model, we show that this conventional wisdom can be overturned when a supplier is dual channel: operating a direct channel that sells to end customers in addition to an indirect channel that sells to an industry peer who serves the same market. Compared with zero trade credit provision where the supplier requires cash on delivery (COD), we observe empirically that high trade credit provision can lead to lower risk for the dual-channel supplier. We propose a possible mechanism for this risk mitigation effect—pooling: When the market overlap between the supplier and its peer buyer is sufficiently high, the random split of the overlapping market creates negative association between the supplier’s direct channel sales and the buyer’s trade credit payment. Trade credit does not always mitigate risk for dual-channel suppliers. If the supplier’s debt level is high, our theory predicts that trade credit exacerbates risk. We find empirical evidence consistent with our theoretical predictions using data on U.S. manufacturing firms that sell to their industry peers. The positive association between trade credit provision and bankruptcy risk is dampened or even reversed once a supplier begins selling to peer firms. This risk mitigation effect is stronger among suppliers with lower leverage and greater market overlap with their buyers. For highly financially constrained suppliers, trade credit provision is associated with an increase in bankruptcy risk after the supplier becomes dual channel. This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03142 .

title: Correcting the Unobserved Textual Confounding Factors in Regression by BERT and Partially Linear Regression
authors: Mengke Qiao; Ke-Wei Huang
affiliations: Culverhouse College of Business, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Alabama 35487; School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119077
abstract: In the last decade, there has been a surge of text-mining applications in the information systems literature. In these applications, researchers typically construct independent variables from documents by various text-mining techniques. The most prominent example could be using online review sentiments to investigate online word-of-mouth issues. Typically, most documents contain information richer than the independent variable, and researchers may construct control variables from the same documents to alleviate endogeneity issues. However, researchers need to manually craft these variables, and this process may not guarantee that all the important confounding factors are extracted and included in the regression model with a correct functional form. If useful textual information is overlooked and a valid identification strategy is not available, the omitted variable bias may occur. To solve this challenge, we propose a novel model that utilizes text embedding based on the state-of-the-art neural network language model (i.e., bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)) to automatically create a new control variable vector for controlling latent confounding factors in the absence of a valid identification strategy. Moreover, our approach can be considered a semiparametric approach in that our model contains a linear term of the key independent variable and an unknown functional term of the textual control variables. Our approach extends the semiparametric framework, double machine learning, by introducing a novel Neyman-orthogonal loss function in an integrated deep neural network to minimize the estimation bias. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of controlling textual control variables by text embedding and improving the estimation performance by the novel loss function. This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04758 .

title: Inferential Theory for Pricing Errors with Latent Factors and Firm Characteristics
authors: Jungjun Choi; Ming Yuan
affiliations: Department of Computer Science and Statistics, University of Rhode Island, Kingston, Rhode Island 02881; Department of Statistics, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
abstract: We study factor models that combine latent factors with firm characteristics and propose a new framework for modeling, estimating, and inferring pricing errors. Following Zhang (2024), our approach decomposes mispricing into two distinct components: inside alpha, explained by firm characteristics but orthogonal to factor exposures, and outside alpha, orthogonal to both factors and characteristics. Our model generalizes those developed recently such as Kelly et al. (2019) and Zhang (2024), resolving issues of orthogonality, basis dependence, and unit sensitivity. Methodologically, we develop estimators grounded in low-rank methods with explicit debiasing, providing closed-form solutions and a rigorous inferential theory that accommodates a growing number of characteristics and relaxes standard assumptions on sample dimensions. Empirically, using U.S. stock returns from 2000 to 2019, we document strong evidence of both inside and outside alphas, with the former showing industry-level comovements and the latter reflecting idiosyncratic shocks beyond firm fundamentals. Our framework thus unifies statistical and characteristic-based approaches to factor modeling, offering both theoretical advances and new insights into the structure of pricing errors. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grant DMS-2052955]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04971 .

title: Echoes of Discord: The Effects of Global Conflicts and Disputes on Entrepreneurship
authors: Astrid Marinoni
affiliations: Scheller College of Business, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30308
abstract: Mixed-nationality founding teams bring together heterogeneous, hard-to-replicate bundles of human capital and country-specific ties through their cross-national networks, providing a distinctive foundation for building successful ventures. Yet these connections may be vulnerable to nonmarket shocks. This study examines whether geopolitical conflicts and disputes between the countries of origin of immigrant founders affect the formation of new ventures. Leveraging data on the founders of start-ups established in Great Britain and global information on conflicts and disputes, I find that such tensions reduce the likelihood that nationals of hostile countries cofound firms together. The evidence is more consistent with social mechanisms and, particularly, the erosion of interpersonal relationships than with diminished access to cross-country resources or the loss of entrepreneurial opportunities. Start-ups of both low and high quality are affected, including in sectors that depend heavily on skilled human capital, such as high-tech and business services. The negative effect is substantially attenuated for nationality pairs that are heavily colocated across local areas and for founders with prior social exposure to individuals from the opposing nationality, indicating that interpersonal ties can buffer against geopolitical shocks. Conflicts do not affect the exit of existing firms, and the decline in mixed-nationality entrepreneurship is not offset by alternative team configurations such as solo ventures or those formed with conationals, natives, or individuals from third-party countries. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Funding: I gratefully acknowledge funding from the Institute for Leadership and Social Impact at Georgia Institute of Technology. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04559 .

title: Can working from home advance the gender revolution?
authors: Brendan Churchill; Leah Ruppanner
affiliations: School of Social and Political Sciences, The University of Melbourne, Australia
abstract: Working from home provides a critical test case for the second half of the gender revolution: whether bringing paid work into the home increases men’s involvement in care and produces more equitable domestic arrangements. Drawing on 18 waves of the HILDA Survey (2005–2022), this article uses Mundlak hybrid models to examine associations between working from home and mothers’ and fathers’ unpaid labour, time pressure, satisfaction with partner and task divisions, and perceived fairness in childcare and housework, distinguishing within-person changes from between-person differences. Working from home is associated with more housework for mothers and fathers and increased care time for fathers, while mothers who work from home remain embedded in higher-care arrangements. It is also associated with greater time pressure, particularly for fathers, while women with greater overall exposure report greater unfairness in childcare and housework, suggesting that working from home may increase fathers’ involvement without transforming unequal domestic arrangements.

title: A Unified Resilience Evaluation Framework for Markov‐Type Based Multi‐State Systems
authors: Meiyan Li; Bei Wu; Nikolaos Limnios; Xiangyu Qin
affiliations: School of Management Northwestern Polytechnical University Xi'an China; Laboratory of Applied Mathematics of Compiègne University of Technology of Compiègne Compiègne France
abstract: ABSTRACT Resilience has emerged as a fundamental attribute in the design and management of complex systems, reflecting the growing recognition that systems must not only resist disruptions but also recover effectively. While conceptual advances have been substantial, the quantification of resilience in a manner that integrates both capacities remains an open challenge. To address this gap, this paper introduces a unified resilience evaluation framework for multi‐state systems exposed to single or multiple hazards, whose performance evolution is characterized using four Markov‐type models: Markov chains, semi‐Markov chains, Markov processes, and semi‐Markov processes. Two resilience dimensions, namely absorptive and restorative resilience, are defined to quantify the capacity of the system to withstand disruptions and restore functionality, respectively. For each dimension, both static and dynamic metrics are proposed to capture pathway‐based probabilities and time‐dependent behaviors. Analytical formulas are derived for all resilience metrics and subsequently verified through simulation‐based algorithms. The applicability of the models and metrics is demonstrated through two case studies: a building portfolio and a nuclear power plant, both subjected to earthquake hazards. The findings illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed fram ework in characterizing multi‐state system resilience, with practical implications for system design and risk management.

title: When Critical Roads Fail: Nonlinear Impacts of Flooding on Network Connectivity and Community Resilience
authors: Shun Cao; Hiroki Sayama; Changqing Cheng
affiliations: School of Management State University of New York Binghamton New York USA; School of Systems Science and Industrial Engineering State University of New York Binghamton New York USA; Waseda Innovation Lab Waseda University Tokyo Japan
abstract: ABSTRACT Flooding is among the most disruptive hazards to community access, severing mobility lifelines and isolating residential areas from essential services. This study addresses that gap by integrating an inundation model with percolation analysis to evaluate how floods reshape network connectivity, efficiency, and service accessibility. With the illustrative example of Broome County, NY, we simulated progressive road inundation based on elevation and traced cascading effects on network connectivity, efficiency, and service access. Results revealed that while fewer than 20% of roads are directly inundated, the modeled network exhibits an abrupt transition within an approximate elevation band near 263–264 m under the present modeling assumptions. At this threshold, the failure of a few cross‐valley connectors fragments the network, reduces efficiency by about 60%, disconnects more than 80% of the predefined analyzed origin–destination pairs, and cuts off access to emergency services. Accessibility loss follows a service‐specific sequence, with police access deteriorating first, followed by fire stations and hospitals. A qualitative comparison with historical impact data provides contextual support for the broad spatial patterns produced by the model. Because the framework requires only digital elevation models and open‐source road data, it is computationally efficient and globally transferable. By reframing flood impacts as nonlinear percolation processes, it provides network‐level insights and practical guidance for protecting strategic bottlenecks and sustaining community access under extreme events.

title: Toward More Resilient Community: Unveiling Information Dissemination Mode of Disaster Risk by a Social Network Approach
authors: Feiting Gao; Li Peng; Damin Zhou; Juntao Sun; Pei Huang
affiliations: College of Geography and Resources Sichuan Normal University Chengdu China; Key Laboratory of Land Resources Evaluation and Monitoring in Southwest Ministry of Education Sichuan Normal University Chengdu China
abstract: ABSTRACT The timely, clear, and accurate dissemination of geo‐disaster information to the public is a critical component of climate adaptation and disaster response strategies. However, behavioral inertia and the amplification of misinformation pose major challenges to risk communication in rural areas, hindering effective climate resilience building. In this study, survey data were collected from 536 rural households in the Longmen Mountain region in southwest China, which is an area frequently threatened by geohazards exacerbated by changing climate patterns. Social network analysis (SNA) was applied to explore how formal and informal communication channels influence household response behaviors. A novel channel–behavior model was developed to analyze the differences in information dissemination for risk communication and rumor propagation. The results showed that formal communication channels such as village broadcasting dominated risk communication and were more likely to trigger collective action, serving as a vital policy instrument for local governance. In contrast, rumor propagation was primarily driven by informal communication channels such as the internet. Communities were divided into two specific types: passively receptive and risk‐accumulating. Passively receptive communities showed high internal cohesion and rapid norm dissemination while risk‐accumulating communities exhibited fragmented structures that impeded information dissemination and increased vulnerability. The results demonstrate the utility of integrating SNA into human‐environment geography and provide actionable insights for designing spatially sensitive, community‐tailored risk communication policies to enhance climate resilience in rural China.

title: When Human Nature and AI Collide: Identifying Emergent Biases in Risk Management Through Netnography
authors: Helmi Issa
affiliations: AI and Decision Sciences ESSCA School of Management Angers France
abstract: ABSTRACT As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support expert judgment in risk management, the interaction between human and machine generates unintended consequences in the form of emergent biases that distort decision‐making and undermine risk assessments. Taking human–AI teaming as the unit of analysis, this study investigates how collaborative judgment produces biases that neither human error nor software failure alone can explain. Through a netnographic analysis of publicly available podcasts, complemented by three documented case studies, it identifies a cascading, self‐reinforcing cycle of emergent biases (AI Washing [macro‐organizational], Validation [meso‐behavioral], and Off‐Loading [micro‐cognitive]) and the structural interventions (independent benchmarking, temporal separation, and vendor/resource decentralization) positioned at each juncture of that cycle. In doing so, the study defines a new category of risk arising specifically from the relationship between human and AI systems, responds to urgent calls in the risk management literature, and offers organizations a preliminary calibration mechanism for interrupting the bias cascade in AI‐augmented decision environments.

title: Order‐of‐Magnitude Assessment of Strategies to Reduce Risks to Residential Electricity Customers From Tropical Cyclones
authors: Maryam Hamidi; M. Granger Morgan
affiliations: Department of Engineering and Public Policy Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Power distribution systems face increasing risks from tropical cyclones (TCs or hurricanes), which can cause prolonged outages and serious social and economic impacts. While there are models to assess distribution system resilience, they are typically complex and highly location specific. Many smaller utilities, such as co‐ops, lack the resources to develop such frameworks and perform detailed analysis to evaluate distribution system resilience strategies such as pole upgrades. In this paper, we illustrate an order‐of‐magnitude approach that employs stochastic simulation using historical hurricane records and power pole fragility curves for wood power poles to estimate the expected value of replacing wood poles with composite poles which bend, but do not break, under hurricane winds. In an illustration of the method applied to the mid‐Atlantic coast, we find that over a 40‐year period replacing wood poles that have been damaged by TCs with composite poles shows substantial economic advantages over replacement with new wood poles. In this illustration, customer density and geographic TC risk emerge as the primary economic drivers, with coastal suburban feeders showing the greatest benefits across the four feeder types modeled. Total 40‐year cost reductions range from about 18% to 37%, reaching $4.7 million in the highest‐risk coastal suburban scenario. We conclude by noting that a similar order‐of‐magnitude strategy could be adapted and used by utilities and others to assess other risks to distribution systems.

title: Occupational Safety and Health Risks of Augmented Reality at Work: A Literature Review and Interview Study
authors: Simone Grassini
affiliations: Department of Psychosocial Science University of Bergen, Bergen, Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Augmented reality (AR) is increasingly used in manufacturing, logistics, construction, energy, and healthcare to provide workers with hands‐free, task‐specific information. The impact of AR on occupational safety and health (OSH) is still being evaluated. This paper reviews the existing literature on AR‐specific OSH risks and looks at how these are experienced and managed at work. A structured literature review (an initial search covering 2016 to 2023 and an update search to October 2026) was combined with semi‐structured interviews with seven experts from OSH consultancy, labor inspection, industrial safety management, AR development, and frontline supervision. The risks fall into four overlapping areas: perceptual and cognitive (attention being drawn to the display, failure to notice hazards, misplaced virtual content, and over‐reliance on guidance), physical and ergonomic (weight of the headset, reduced blink rate and eye strain, motion sickness with moving content, and battery hazards), psychosocial (stress, isolation and deskilling, with very little evidence in the AR‐specific literature), and privacy and security (continuous sensing of workers, co‐workers, and proprietary processes). The quantitative findings indicate that the perceptual, performance and physiological effects studied are measurable during short exposures but that such evidence is often based on small samples and short tasks. The interviewees also identified these risks and raised organizational concerns: Formal risk assessments were rare (recorded in only one deployment), compatibility with personal protective equipment needed to be checked, devices assessed for one application were expected to be reused in others without reassessment, and standardization and certification were uneven. The paper concludes with AR‐specific risk‐assessment items, design principles and governance priorities, and a research agenda.

title: Expert Judgments of Residual Risk in Three New Zealand Rural High‐Speed Work‐Zone Scenarios
authors: Dave Tilton; Jacobus Daniel van der Walt
affiliations: Department of Civil and Natural Resources Engineering University of Canterbury Christchurch New Zealand
abstract: ABSTRACT New Zealand's move from prescribed layouts toward site‐specific work‐zone risk assessment raises questions about the evidence supporting event‐frequency judgments. We elicited distributions from 36 practitioners for event return periods, conditional severities, and risk multipliers in three rural high‐speed work‐zone scenarios. Participants estimated privately before and after facilitated discussion and anonymized feedback. We pooled their distributions with equal weights. Frequency judgments differed by orders of magnitude and were strongly structured by workshop membership. The Christchurch workshop's median participant return periods exceeded the combined median of the other two workshops on all 12 events (median ratio 13); the Auckland workshops were at or below the combined median of the others on all 12 (median ratio 0.05). In a post hoc descriptive comparison, the median between‐workshop share of squared deviations in log return‐period medians rose from 0.25 before scenario discussion and feedback to 0.76 afterward. This does not establish an effect of deliberation. Inconsistent instructions left the multiplier risk quantity unresolved, and one event had conflicting exposure units. Reference questions lacked fixed realized values, preventing calibration, and no configuration‐matched outcomes validated the judgments. The contribution includes documenting closer agreement within these workshops alongside persistent disagreement between them, and diagnosing limits of the elicitation. The estimates are insufficiently validated for operational use. We recommend shared event and exposure definitions, prospective linked records, validation of intermediate measures, and evaluation of assessment methods used in practice.

title: Beyond Events: Infrastructure as Sociomaterial Signals for Knowing Flood Risk in the Present
authors: Noémia Salgado Cunha
affiliations: Miguel Torga Higher Institute Coimbra Portugal
abstract: ABSTRACT Flood risk has predominantly been conceptualized through future‐oriented regimes of anticipation and is typically recognized only as extreme events approach. This article challenges that framing by reconceptualizing risk as a sociomaterial process that becomes empirically legible in the present through recurring patterns embedded in the everyday functioning of infrastructures. Drawing on prolonged field observation, documentary analysis, and engagement with local actors, it introduces the concept of sociomaterial signals of risk, redefines infrastructures as epistemically active artifacts, and develops an understanding of risk grounded in situated interpretations of infrastructural functioning. For disaster studies, this approach expands what counts as evidence for risk governance, supporting earlier and territorially situated forms of intervention. In doing so, the article redefines the conditions under which risk becomes governable, through the stabilization of recurring sociomaterial signals in everyday infrastructural functioning.

title: Epistemic Monoculture in Risk Assessment: Common‐Cause Blind Spots in Human–AI Teaming
authors: Milad Baghersad; C. Derrick Huang
affiliations: Department of Information Technology & Operations Management, College of Business Florida Atlantic University Boca Raton Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The value of redundancy in risk assessment depends not only on individual assessor accuracy, but also on whether assessment errors remain sufficiently independent. This paper studies how human–AI teaming can weaken that independence when multiple assessors rely on the same or similar AI systems. We develop a formal model of AI‐assisted assessors evaluating a common set of hazards. Each assessor combines its own independent judgment with shared AI‐generated advice. The AI signal may contain random error and class‐specific omission bias for hazards that are rare, novel, or poorly represented in the AI system's information environment. The model identifies an accuracy–correlation trade‐off: Greater reliance on AI can reduce individual mean squared error while making assessors' errors more correlated. When AI advice contains omission bias, greater reliance can also pull multiple assessors' estimates below the escalation threshold for the same hazard class. We derive the individual miss probability, the systemic miss probability that all assessors miss a hazard, the diversity dividend, and the homogenization ratio. The results show that evaluating AI assistance only by individual accuracy can be misleading. Even when AI assistance lowers each assessor's miss probability, it can increase the probability that all assessors miss the same hazard if the added correlation in their errors outweighs the individual accuracy gain. The analysis highlights the importance of system‐level evaluation and suggests that pre‐AI elicitation, diversified AI inputs, and audits of correlated omissions can help preserve the redundancy benefit of multiple assessments.

abstract: ABSTRACT This review assesses Daniel Berliner's Learning from the Public, which treats the processing of citizen input as a neglected stage of participation. Its typology of processing is valuable for research and practice. However, the evidence is illustrative; the book does not separate weak capacity from unwillingness to listen, and thin coverage of the global South limits its general claims.

title: Growing, but Not Necessarily Showing: Pregnancy in Remote Versus In‐Person Contexts
authors: Aashna M. Waiwood; Tammy D. Allen; Alyssa M. Lezcano; Joseph Regina
affiliations: U.S. Department of Defense Washington DC USA; University of South Florida Tampa Florida USA; Rutgers University Camden New Jersey USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Pregnancy is a stigmatized state in the workplace, and research has increasingly documented the unique experience of being pregnant at work, including difficulties with pregnancy disclosure. Theory and research seemingly take as a given that women's pregnancies are visible or that they become visible. Moreover, visibility appears crucial to explaining pregnancy‐related experiences, behaviors, and treatment. However, working remotely alters the presumed inevitability of visibility. Based on qualitative and quantitative data, we explore how working remotely corresponds with women's disclosure and postdisclosure pregnancy‐related perceptions, decisions, and experiences. Findings demonstrate that time working remotely is associated with greater perceptions of disclosure control, disclosure to a narrower network, delayed disclosure timing, and reduced need to disclose for transparency purposes. In the postdisclosure period, time working remotely is related to reduced conspicuousness of the “unseemly” pregnant body and its symptoms, or fewer physical “reminders,” of one's pregnancy and pregnancy‐related behaviors, corresponding with reduced awareness, addressing, and comments (often invasive in nature) on one's pregnant status by others. Results support the importance of accounting for stigma visibility and obtrusiveness in existing theories and have implications for the use of remote work or other visibility‐linked strategies to address pregnancy experiences.

title: Can Workplace Creativity Increase Positive Affect Through Absorption? The Moderating Roles of Negative Affect and Competitive Climate
authors: March L. To; Gillian Yeo; Cynthia D. Fisher
affiliations: School of Management, College of Business and Law RMIT University Melbourne Australia; University of Western Australia Perth Australia; Bond University Gold Coast Australia
abstract: ABSTRACT Workplace creativity is often studied as an outcome influenced by employees' affective states. There is growing interest in the potential for creative activity to improve positive affect, but there is insufficient knowledge about when or why such activity may change how employees feel at work. We draw on affect regulation theory to consider the mechanisms and boundary conditions involved in the relationship between creative process engagement (CPE) and changes in positive affect. We suggest that engaging in creative processes at work has the potential to increase positive affect through increased task absorption. However, our framework highlights that these effects of CPE are contingent on two factors: the accompanying negative affect and the surrounding competitive climate for creativity. We develop progressive support for our predictions in a laboratory experiment followed by a field experience sampling study. The laboratory study found that CPE increased positive affect through greater task absorption when negative affect was high. The field study tested and supported our full model, with competitive climate for creativity impacting the moderated‐mediated relationship, such that it weakened the CPE × negative affect interactive effect on increasing positive affect via task absorption.

title: Moral Licensing Revisited: CSR and Cybersecurity‐related Disclosure After COP21
authors: Vu Quang Trinh; Teng Li; Marwa Elnahass; Ngan Duong Cao
affiliations: Newcastle University Business School, Newcastle University Newcastle upon Tyne NE1 7RU UK; Essex Business School University of Essex Colchester CO4 3SQ UK; Department of Accounting and Finance King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals Dhahran Saudi Arabia; Interdisciplinary Research Center for Hydrogen Technologies and Carbon Management King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals Dhahran Saudi Arabia; University of Bath School of Management Bath BA2 7AY UK
abstract: Abstract Using a sample of U.S. S&P 100 firms, we examine the relationship between firms’ CSR and cybersecurity‐related disclosure, exploiting the 2015 Paris Climate Conference (COP21) as an institutional shock in a difference‐in‐differences design. We find that, prior to COP21, firms’ aggregated environmental and social (E&S) profiles, and environmental (E) profiles are negatively but not significantly associated with cybersecurity‐related disclosure, whereas social (S) profiles exhibit a significantly negative association. Drawing on moral licensing theory, we argue that firm leaders who perceive their firms as having accumulated sufficient moral capital through CSR engagement may feel less compelled to respond proactively to emerging stakeholder expectations in non‐traditional responsibility domains such as cybersecurity. Following COP21, however, firms with stronger aggregated E&S, E, and S profiles increase their cybersecurity‐related disclosure. We interpret COP21 as an institutional inflection point that intensified scrutiny and strengthened evaluative standards surrounding corporate sustainability, thereby diminishing the protective value of previously accrued moral credentials. Under heightened accountability, firm leaders appear more inclined to reaffirm a responsible organizational identity through greater transparency and responsiveness to stakeholder information demands. Overall, our evidence suggests that greater cybersecurity‐related disclosure may help firms signal their commitment to cybersecurity and reinforce their socially legitimate identity.

title: Territory‐as‐pedagogy: Learning with the Territorial Imaginaries of Rural and Indigenous Students in Management Education
authors: Ana Laura Dominguez Paredes; Rajiv Maher; Clara Toxqui Teutle
affiliations: Facultad de Responsabilidad Social Universidad Anáhuac México Norte Huixquilucan Mexico; Egade Business School Tecnologico de Monterrey Ciudad de México 01389 Mexico; Instituto de Ciencias Sociales y Humanidades‐BUAP Heroica Puebla de Zaragoza 72000 Mexico
abstract: Abstract Business schools are being asked to prepare managers for a climate‐altered world, and that debate has centered largely on what curricula contain, paying less attention to territory as an epistemic and pedagogical category, or to the students whose territorial knowledge sits outside dominant models. Drawing on an interpretive study with rural and Indigenous scholarship students at a private Mexican university, in which participant‐produced drawings were read alongside interviews and social‐cartography workshops, we ask how the territorial imaginaries of students from rural and Indigenous communities might inform more epistemically just curricula in business schools. We read the drawings as expressing five recurring territorial imaginaries that cohere into four themes and compose a relational territorial imaginary. Consequently, we advance the concept of territory‐as‐pedagogy, an account of territory as a co‐teacher that supplies the terms of economic and ethical reasoning rather than serving as a backdrop. We contend that territory‐as‐pedagogy makes ecological limits and obligation visible because students reason from relations and ties they hold to land, water, crops and kin, which a module added to a curriculum would struggle to reproduce. We propose it as a context‐specific resource for educators, stating a limit of place‐based pedagogy and contributing to decolonial and Indigenous management scholarship.

title: Parsimonious theorizing
authors: Diego Jannace; Saeid Kazemi; Arnaldo Camuffo
affiliations: Entrepreneurship and Family Enterprise INSEAD Singapore Singapore; ION Management Science Lab‐SDA Bocconi Bocconi University Milan Italy; Department of Economics and Decision Sciences HEC Paris Paris France; Department of Management and Technology Bocconi University Milan Italy
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs act on theories of value, and the theory‐based view favors simplicity. Yet a theory can be too thin to guide action or too heavy to carry, and simplicity cannot tell which. We model a theory as bundles linking attempted actions, uncertain implementation states, and external conditions to a focal outcome, and make its structure a choice variable. Parsimony then calls for optimal rather than minimal complexity: structure whose contribution to the value of acting justifies its carrying cost. Under the model's assumptions, optimal complexity rises with value at stake, representational capacity, and domain knowledge, and falls with bundle overlap. Theories also change. The entrepreneur's theory shapes her awareness, so some bundles are worth carrying for what they open, while commitments make revision path dependent. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often need to explain a future that does not yet exist: what they will try, what must work, and why customers, partners, or investors should care. We show how to weigh the value of linked actions, their possible results, and outside conditions against the effort of understanding, communicating, and testing them. More detail is worthwhile when the potential payoff is greater, the entrepreneur knows the business better, or the team can handle complexity; overlapping ideas add less. As evidence accumulates, the theory may need to expand, shrink, or be rebuilt. Some ideas are worth keeping because they reveal new possibilities. Earlier investments can make changes costly, so a failed test may call for reshaping the idea rather than abandoning it.

title: Domestic Tariffs and Consumer Welfare in Developing Countries: Evidence From India
authors: Jerónimo Callejas; Chirantan Chatterjee; Debi Prasad Mohapatra
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst Massachusetts USA; Department of Economics University of Sussex Business School Brighton UK
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the welfare consequences of industrial policies aimed at boosting domestic manufacturing in developing countries, focusing on the Indian government's tariff policy for mobile handset production. We develop a structural model of India's mobile handset industry, where firms endogenously decide supply chain alternatives, product sets, and prices. Our counterfactual simulations indicate that the status quo import tariff on ready‐to‐use handsets significantly increases local assembly operations. However, a lower tariff of around 8% would maintain similar assembly levels and significantly enhance consumer surplus. An additional input import tariff on handset components discourages firms from relocating operations to India, potentially undermining the policy's goal.

title: A Signal-Extraction Theory of Inflation Pass-Through
authors: Engin Kara
affiliations: Cardiff Business School, University of Cardiff , Cardiff, CF10 3EU ,
abstract: Abstract I develop a theory of state-dependent signal extraction in price setting. Firms infer how much sectoral price movements reflect persistent aggregate or transitory sector-specific disturbances. When inflation is low relative to sectoral variation, sticky-price firms discount competitor movements because following transitory movements risks leaving them mispriced. As inflation rises relative to sectoral noise, firms increasingly attribute these movements to aggregate shocks and sticky firms respond more strongly. UK micro-price data support these predictions: below approximately 1.9% sectoral inflation, sticky firms respond less to competitors than flexible firms; above it, the gap closes. This convergence generates state-dependent aggregate inflation dynamics.

title: XBRL adoption and SEC monitoring
authors: Minjae Koo; Yinqi Zhang; Meiling Zhao; Yuping Zhao
abstract: Abstract We examine how disclosure processing costs influence SEC monitoring of firm disclosures by leveraging the mandatory adoption of XBRL—a digital reporting language designed to reduce these costs. Post adoption, both the frequency and quality of SEC comment letters for 10-K filings increase. Additional tests suggest that XBRL enhances SEC monitoring through three channels. First, automated data extraction improves review efficiency, as reflected in more timely comment letters and greater XBRL benefits when the SEC faces tighter resource constraints or uses XBRL analytical tools. Second, standardized reporting strengthens the SEC’s benchmarking ability: firms using more standardized tags and tags more comparable to those of industry peers benefit more. Third, XBRL facilitates SEC scrutiny of complex reporting issues, yielding more frequent and higher-quality comments on noncore earnings accounts and for firms with more footnote tags or complex filings. Overall, our evidence suggests that reduced disclosure processing costs enhance the SEC’s regulatory monitoring.

title: Blood is Still Thicker Than Water: A Response to Lin’s Reappraisal and Reflections on Historical Political Economy
authors: YUHUA WANG
affiliations: Harvard University
abstract: A recent reappraisal by Lin expands Wang’s (2022, American Political Science Review 116, 896–910) dataset and questions the robustness of its main finding. In this response, I clarify broader challenges of measurement, case selection, and inference in historical political economy. I show that my original finding—that kinship-network concentration is negatively associated with support for state-building reforms—remains robust across multiple coding strategies. I also acknowledge that two high-leverage cases, the Lü brothers, matter for inference; rather than treating them as removable anomalies, I argue that their extreme values are theoretically meaningful features of kinship-network structure. Finally, I engage Lin’s regional interpretation and show that regional status competition does not account for the observed relationship once measurement and estimation issues are addressed. More broadly, this exchange illustrates how transparent measurement and sustained dialogue between quantitative and qualitative evidence can generate cumulative knowledge from fragmentary historical archives.

title: Do Politicians’ Errors in Understanding Public Opinion Persist When They Encounter Individual Constituents?
authors: JACK LUCAS; LIOR SHEFFER; NOAM TITELMAN
affiliations: University of Calgary; Tel Aviv University
abstract: When thinking about public opinion, politicians commonly exhibit three general perceptual errors: a tendency to overestimate their constituents’ conservatism ( conservative bias ), a tendency to hold more accurate knowledge of privileged constituents than constituents in general ( privilege bias ), and a tendency to overestimate how much their constituents share their views ( projection bias ). Studies documenting these patterns invariably rely on assessing politicians’ perceptions of aggregated public opinion. In practice, however, politicians heavily prioritize and rely on the opinions of individual constituents, raising concerns about the external validity of these findings. Thus, in this article, we explore whether politicians’ common perceptual errors persist when they think about specific individual constituents, rather than aggregate public opinion. We assign more than 1,400 Canadian politicians to predict the ideology and issue positions of more than 4,000 randomly generated citizen profiles that vary by a host of salient sociodemographic and political factors. We then compare their evaluations to estimates of these citizens’ real-life positions drawn from a general population survey. We find that politicians do not exhibit conservative bias or privilege bias when making inferences about individual constituents. However, even when thinking about individual constituents, projection bias persists, and the perception errors it creates are amplified when politicians are more similar to their constituents. We discuss the implications of these findings for theories of political representation.

title: Conspiracy theory communication framing and support for antidemocratic behavior
authors: Frances Cayton; Courtney Blackington
affiliations: Center on Democracy, Development, and the Rule of Law Stanford University Stanford California USA; Department of Political Science University of Pittsburgh Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA
abstract: Abstract Many politicians use conspiracy theories (CTs) to win electoral support and justify antidemocratic policies. How do individuals evaluate this strategy? We theorize and show that variation in CT communication frames affects individuals’ willingness to endorse antidemocratic policies and politicians. Politicians who explicitly appeal to a CT earn greater support for antidemocratic behavior than those using implicit appeals. However, this effect primarily occurs for novel CTs lacking partisan cues. Over time, as CTs become more politicized, they lose their mobilizational capacity and can reduce support for CT‐wielding politicians—even among co‐partisans. Three preregistered survey experiments surrounding the 2023 parliamentary and 2025 presidential elections in Poland, and survey data from 21 countries, provide empirical support for our theory. Ultimately, we show that CTs alone are not always enough to justify attacks on democratic norms and institutions to the public.

title: Regional Deprivation, Individual Prospects, and Political Resentment
authors: Giovanni Facchini; Anja Neundorf; Sergi Pardos-Prado; Cecilia Testa
affiliations: University of Nottingham and Centre for Economic Policy Research; University of Glasgow
abstract: Abstract Regional economic conditions are well-established determinants of the geography of political resentment. However, regions are not homogeneous, and the mechanisms through which local economies affect individual political attitudes are unclear. We argue that feelings of relative deprivation are shaped by how personal prospects are tied to regional conditions, and that the interaction between subjective individual and regional deprivation affects perceptions of shared struggle and systemic unfairness. Through a large-scale survey experiment in Britain addressing geographical self-selection, we provide causal evidence that poor individuals in poor regions express political resentment, whereas in affluent regions the political attitudes of poor and wealthy individuals are indistinguishable. Our findings stress (1) the importance of egocentric mechanisms whereby local economies shape individual prospects; (2) the significance of subjective beliefs over objective information on deprivation; (3) the mobilization potential of highlighting regional deprivation by political entrepreneurs; and (4) the relevance of place-based policies to mitigate political discontent.

title: Breaking into the Public Sphere: How Protest Tactics Shape Media Visibility
authors: Michael Jacobs
affiliations: ETH Zurich: Eidgenossische Technische Hochschule Zurich
abstract: Abstract Getting heard is a crucial first step for protesters to influence policy and public opinion. How can protest organisers boost their coverage in the media? This study provides new evidence on this question, based on a decade of UK environmental and economic protests from 2010 to 2020 ( N = 1,708). Relying on protest groups’ social media streams as trace data, I introduce a computer-assisted method for constructing a media-independent protest event dataset. Using a ‘within-group’ design, I provide a sharper test of the causal effects of tactical choices compared to previous studies. I find that confrontational elements, such as disruption and arrests, are the strongest predictors, more than doubling the expected magnitude of coverage. I also find that right-leaning (ideologically unsympathetic) outlets are more responsive to confrontational elements than left-leaning (ideologically sympathetic) outlets, which suggests that disruptive tactics affect the composition as well as the size of a protest’s audience.

title: INO volume 80 issue 4 Cover and Front matter
INO volume 80 issue 4 Cover and Back matter
The Dependence Dilemma: Engagement, Vulnerability, and the Politics of Derisking
authors: Brett V. Benson; Haonan Dong; Bradley C. Smith
affiliations: Vanderbilt University; Princeton University
abstract: Abstract What makes economic interdependence a force for peace rather than a source of strategic vulnerability? We argue that interdependence generates both pacifying opportunity costs and dangerous dependence, and the tension between these two forces is the key to understanding when economic engagement promotes peace and when it provokes war. We develop a dynamic model of economic dependence and conflict that generates both the pacifying and conflict-inducing effects of interdependence within a single unified framework. We show that states use “derisking” as a strategic middle path, selectively restricting economic engagement to reset future leverage without destroying the gains from exchange that make peace valuable. The theory explains why dependence-driven wars are rare yet possible. Forward-looking leaders prefer incurring the costs of economic restraint to the catastrophic risks of conflict. When derisking is structurally foreclosed or restrictions destroy too much economic value, the commitment problem cannot be managed through policy and preventive war may occur.

title: Territory Without Centralization: Conflicting Spatial Ideologies of the Shogunate, Domains, and Villages in Early Modern Japan
authors: Naosuke Mukoyama
affiliations: University of Tokyo
abstract: Abstract This article reconceptualizes the formation of territory by examining early modern Japan, showing that territory can emerge through bottom-up processes without centralization. Contrary to dominant narratives based on European history that portray territory as a product of top-down projects, the Japanese case reveals that multiple levels of political actors—the Tokugawa shogunate, individual domains, and village communities—held competing spatial ideologies and engaged in struggles over how space should be organized and governed, and as a result, territory emerged without centralization. The shogunate sought to impose a vision of a unified territory through land surveys and repeated production of provincial maps. However, because it lacked the capacity to carry out these projects directly, implementation depended on domains, inadvertently strengthening their territorial demarcation and autonomy. Yet domains themselves could not fully impose their spatial conceptions onto the population. Because land surveys focused only on cultivated fields, the delineation of boundaries in uncultivated areas was driven by peasants whose need for access to common resources such as grasslands and timber motivated numerous inter-village disputes. Through boundary disputes, villages played a central role in defining the borders that ultimately structured domanial territories. This article contributes to international relations scholarship by revising the dominant state-centric view of territory and state formation, casting doubt on the effectiveness of war making and map making in the process of state formation, demonstrating that territorial formation need not coincide with sovereignty, and advancing our understanding of non-European historical international order.
